I am seventy years old and have farmed this land in Quzhou County my whole life. I never went to school, but I know our soil and weather better than any book. I have four mu of good flat land on the North China Plain. My children work in the city, so I manage the fields myself, though neighbors help me during the busy harvest and planting weeks.

This year I will stick to what I know: **winter wheat followed by summer maize**. That is the rotation everyone around here relies on, and at my age I do not have the strength or the courage to try cotton or vegetables, which need more spraying, weeding, and picking. The wheat is sown in October, sleeps through the winter, and is harvested in early June. Immediately after threshing, I plant the maize without ploughing—no-tillage saves my back and catches the summer rains and heat. The maize is ready by October.

For the wheat, I will rotary-till the field and sow about thirty jin of improved wheat seed per mu. I will spread roughly one hundred jin of compound fertilizer as a basal dose, and top-dress with urea in spring when the wheat greens up. I will irrigate three times: once before winter to help the seedlings survive the cold, once at jointing when the stems shoot up, and once at grain filling. I will spray pesticides two or three times when I see aphids or too many weeds.

For the maize, I will use hybrid seed—about one package per mu—and put down eighty jin of compound fertilizer at planting. Maize usually needs two irrigations in summer if the rains are light. I will watch for corn borers and spray two or three times when the neighbors start spraying.

This plan gives me enough grain to eat, straw for fuel and fodder, and a little cash from selling the surplus. It is safe, familiar, and within what these old hands can still manage.
